results.summary: This design implements a simple traffic light sequence that cycles through red, red-yellow, green, and yellow states. The sequence is controlled by two input pins, where the binary combination selects the current light state. It is intended as a basic educational example, likely created in the Wokwi simulator. No external hardware is required beyond the chip itself, and the documentation is minimal.

The Logic Test project is a simple design intended to verify basic logic functionality. It has eight input pins and two output pins, but the documentation provides no details on the logic implemented or how the outputs are derived. The design is likely a template or placeholder for testing purposes. There is insufficient documentation to determine its exact behavior or use.

The Abacus Lock is a digital combination lock that activates a servo when a specific sequence of switches is entered. It displays the current combination status in binary on an LED bar. The design is implemented in Wokwi and requires external hardware including LEDs, an LED bar, a servo, and an Arduino Nano. It was sponsored by The MITRE Corporation and MIT/LL Beaverworks Summer Institute.

This project implements a counter that increments from 0 to 99 when a button is pressed, displaying the count on a 7-segment display. Two LEDs indicate whether the current count is even or odd. The design includes modules for button debouncing, counting, and display driving, and is intended for use with the Wokwi simulator. External hardware such as a 7-segment display and LEDs are required.

This design implements an adder with separate flow control for each argument and the result, using a choice of pipeline register/buffer modules. It is a solution to an RTL job interview question and is used in educational repositories. The design includes a self-checking testbench and can be manually tested with buttons and LEDs. It is notable for demonstrating various flow control strategies.

This project is a minimalistic SoC featuring the schoolRISCV educational CPU and a ROM containing a program that computes Fibonacci numbers. The CPU was designed for introductory Verilog and FPGA classes and is based on a textbook. The design outputs the CPU register a0 and program counter bits for observation, along with test pass/fail signals. It requires only LEDs as external hardware.

Sea Battle is a VGA game with sprites where the player controls a torpedo using left and right keys to hit a moving target. It was created for the Tiny Tapeout Demoscene competition and is part of a graphics and music examples repository. The design requires a VGA display and buttons, and has been tested on silicon where it works as an interactive graphics game. There is no self-checking testbench, and the game resets after each round.

SQUARE-1 is a VGA and audio demo that displays munching squares on video and generates audio based on the logistic map. It requires a VGA display and audio output hardware, such as the Tiny VGA and TT Audio Pmods. Silicon tests show that the video works, but audio may require a manual reset and was not consistently heard. The design is notable for combining visual and audio demonstrations in a single project.

Zoom Zoom is a custom CPU with an external memory bus and hardware accelerators for SHA-3 and CORDIC. It includes UART communication and a parallel memory interface. The design is tested by loading a binary program into memory, resetting the chip, and checking memory writes. External hardware such as an SPI RAM chip or an MCU emulator is required for the custom protocol.

This project implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game for VGA display. Players use four directional buttons to slide numbered tiles on a 4x4 grid, merging tiles to reach 2048. The design includes modern and retro color themes and a debug mode for unit testing. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD and has been tested on silicon, where it works as expected.
